title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
description: The /products/search endpoint concatenates the q query parameter directly into a SQL LIKE clause using string concatenation rather than parameterized queries. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the q parameter, bypass filters, extract data from other tables, or drop tables.
evidence: GET /products/search?q='%20OR%201%3D1-- returns all 6 products (HTTP 200) instead of filtering by name. Code at line 41: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%'" + q + "%' ..."

title: Stored XSS via review body rendered with |safe in Jinja2 template
description: Review bodies submitted by authenticated users through POST /products/<id>/reviews are stored in the database and rendered in the HTML template with the |safe filter, which bypasses Jinja2's auto-escaping. A malicious review containing JavaScript executes in any visitor's browser when viewing the product page.
evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with {body: '<script>alert(1)</script>'} returned 201. Subsequent GET /p/MUG-SPECK returns the raw <script> tag unescaped inside the review-body div.

title: Token refresh endpoint accepts forged JWTs (verify_signature=False)
description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes incoming JWTs with jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False}), accepting any arbitrary claims payload regardless of signature. It then creates a new signed Bearer token for whichever user ID appears in the sub claim, enabling privilege escalation.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with fabricated JWT payload {sub: 1, role: 'staff'} returned HTTP 200 with a valid signed Bearer token for user 1. Decoding the response confirms sub=1 and a proper HS256 signature.

title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret in source code
description: SECRET_KEY used to sign and verify JWTs is hardcoded as a plaintext string ('hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'). Anyone with repository access can forge valid tokens for any user identity and role, completely undermining authentication.
evidence: Line 3: SECRET_KEY = \"hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d\" – fixed plaintext string used for both jwt.encode() and jwt.decode() throughout auth.py.

title: Weak password-reset tokens generated with predictable PRNG
description: Password-reset tokens use random.random() (Mersenne Twister, predictable) producing only 8-digit numeric codes (~27 bits of entropy). An attacker who intercepts or leaks a single token can brute-force all codes in minutes. The reset_confirm endpoint performs plain string comparison against this weak token.
evidence: Line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). No cryptographic randomness source (os.urandom/secrets) is used. Space limited to 10^8 possibilities.

title: User account enumeration via login endpoint
description: Login returns different error messages for non-existent accounts ('no account with that email') versus wrong passwords ('wrong password'). An attacker can enumerate registered email addresses by probing the login endpoint with different payloads.
evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@example.com returned {'error': 'no account with that email'}. Same endpoint with priya.shah@mail.test but wrong password returned {'error': 'wrong password'}.

title: Open CORS reflects any Origin with credentials enabled
description: The cors after_request handler sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the requesting Origin without validating against a whitelist, while simultaneously setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Any attacker-controlled site can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the application.
evidence: GET /health with Origin: https://evil.example.com returned Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example.com.

title: Plaintext passwords logged in request bodies for mutating methods
description: The log_request before_request handler logs the full body text of POST, PUT, and PATCH requests up to 2000 characters. This captures passwords from /auth/register, /auth/login, and sensitive PII from other forms.
evidence: Line 31: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]) – captures complete JSON body including the password field during registration and login.

title: Order details exposed via IDOR (insecure direct object reference)
description: GET /orders/<order_id> retrieves and returns full order details using get_order(), which only checks existence—not that the requesting user owns it. Any authenticated user can view another user's orders including items, prices, payment status, and delivery dates.
evidence: Logged in as Priya Shah (user_id=1), GET /orders/3 (owned by user_id=2) returned full order details: items=[BLANKET-WOOL x1], total_pence=4500, delivered_on='2026-10-24'. Compare to /orders list endpoint (line 42) which correctly filters by customer_id.

title: Insecure deserialization of basket cookie via pickle
description: Basket cookies are deserialized using pickle.loads() on fully user-controlled binary data. While post-deserialization validation restricts results to dict type, certain pickle exploit chains can satisfy isinstance(data, dict) while still triggering code execution during unpickling. The cookie has no integrity protection beyond base64 encoding.
evidence: Line 20: data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Accepts user-controlled binary from cookie header. Result validation only checks isinstance(data, dict).

title: Payment confirmation marks unpaid order as paid on provider timeout
description: When confirm-payment times out contacting the provider, the code assumes the payment succeeded (status='paid') and immediately transitions the order to 'processing' (shippable). Network failures, provider outages, or delays cause unpaid orders to ship without actual payment. Losses reconciled overnight per the comment.
evidence: Lines 39-42: except requests.Timeout … status = 'paid', followed by UPDATE SET status='processing' (lines 44-45). No retry or pending state.

title: Gift card redemption has TOCTOU race condition
description: The redeem endpoint reads the gift card balance, validates against it, then updates the balance—all without a transaction. Two concurrent requests from the same user can read the same balance, both pass validation, and both debit the card, resulting in negative effective balance.
evidence: Lines 36-43: Balance is read (line 36), validated (line 39), updated later (line 43) without BEGIN TRANSACTION. Parallel POST /giftcards/redeem requests could double-spend.

title: SQL injection in admin review report via display_name
description: The admin reports/reviews endpoint constructs SQL using f-string interpolation with customer['display_name']. Attackers register with crafted display_names containing SQL metacharacters and trigger injection through this endpoint. Staff authorization protects the route but the token refresh vulnerability makes staff access trivially obtainable.
evidence: Line 80: f\"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC\". Tested: registered user with display_name \"' OR '1'='1\", then requested /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=14 which returned ALL reviews (7 rows) instead of just that customer's.

title: Webhook signature only covers order_id, not event payload
description: The webhook HMAC signature is computed from order_id only. An attacker who learns order_ids (via IDOR or elsewhere) can forge valid webhook signatures with arbitrary status and amount_pence values, marking unpaid orders as paid or forging refund amounts.
evidence: Line 55: hmac.new(secret, str(order_id).encode(), hashlib.sha256). Event data (status, amount_pence) is not part of the signed input but is trusted after signature verification (lines 69-71).

title: Dependencies resolved from internal PyPI index without hash verification
description: Requirements prioritize pypi.hartleyfinch.internal as the primary index with pypi.org as extra-index. No --require-hashes flag is used, meaning package contents are not cryptographically verified against known-good checksums. If the internal PyPI server is compromised, supply-chain injection is possible.
evidence: Line 1: --index-url https://pypi.hartleyfinch.internal/simple (primary). No --require-hashes anywhere. Third-party deps lack hash pinning.

title: Editable local install of hf_payments bypasses supply chain controls
description: The editable install (-e packages/hf_payments) pulls whatever source code exists at that path, bypassing version pinning and hash verification from the dependency index. Combined with lack of --require-hashes on regular deps, this reduces supply chain integrity assurance.
evidence: Line 6: -e packages/hf_payments. Local pyproject.toml uses flit-core with dynamic version from git, confirming mutable local dependency.

title: Flask debug mode enabled (debug=True)
description: run.py runs Flask with debug=True, which enables the interactive debugger accessible via the console and exposes detailed traceback information. On a network-accessible deployment this could allow remote code execution via the debugger PIN feature.

title: Passwords hashed with unsalted SHA-256
description: Passwords are hashed using plain hashlib.sha256 with no salt, no iterations, and no pepper. All users with the same password have identical hashes, making rainbow table attacks practical. This also means the bcrypt/argon2 password_hash column design is wasted.
evidence: Line 16: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). No salt or key stretching applied. Identical passwords produce identical hashes across users.
